proxy-intercept.name: Proxy Intercept: SQLi Bypass
proxy-intercept.description: Use the Proxy Intercept Practice Lab to pause a login request and modify it in transit.

steps.text: Welcome to the Proxy Intercept tutorial! First, click the Email field.
The default email is fine for now.
Click the Submit button. Notice that Intercept is ON, so the request will not go to the server immediately.

The request has been paused! Look at the Intercept window. You'll see the raw HTTP POST request. Let's change the email parameter to a SQL injection payload to bypass the login. Change user@shop.local to admin@shop.local'--
Now click Forward to send the modified request to the server!
Success! The server processed the modified request and granted you admin access because of the SQL injection. Press Next to finish.

proxy-drop.name: Proxy Intercept: Drop Request
proxy-drop.description: Learn how to block malicious or unwanted requests from reaching the server.

steps.text: Sometimes you want to completely block a request from leaving your browser. Click Submit to capture another login request.
The request is caught again. This time, instead of modifying or forwarding it, click the Drop button to destroy the request.
The request was successfully dropped. The server never saw it! Press Next to finish.

proxy-tamper.name: Proxy Intercept: Parameter Tampering
proxy-tamper.description: Learn how to intercept and modify API parameters to manipulate server logic (e.g., getting items for free).

steps.text: Parameter tampering is a classic exploit where you change data sent to the server. Click Submit (Intercept ON) to capture the login request.
The request is paused. This lab's form only sends email and password, so simulate a client-supplied price: add a line "price": 0, inside the JSON body.
Now click Forward to send your manipulated price to the server.
Success! The server trusted the client-supplied price and confirmed the order for 0. Press Next to finish.

proxy-headers.name: Proxy Intercept: Header Manipulation
proxy-headers.description: Learn how to bypass access controls by manipulating HTTP headers like X-Forwarded-For.

steps.text: Servers often use HTTP headers to restrict access. Click Submit (Intercept ON) to capture a request.
The request is caught. The server blocks external IPs, but we can spoof our IP using the X-Forwarded-For header. Add this exact line anywhere in the headers: X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
With the spoofed IP header injected, click Forward to send the request.
Access granted! The server trusted the X-Forwarded-For header and allowed you into the portal. Press Next to finish.

xss-search.name: Reflected XSS: Basic Injection
xss-search.description: Execute a basic Cross-Site Scripting attack using the XSS Sandbox Simulator.

steps.text: Let's test the search functionality for XSS. Click in the payload input field.
Type the standard XSS payload exactly: <script>alert(1)</script>
Now click Inject to send the payload to the server.
Look at the result below! The application reflected your input without sanitization, allowing your script tag to execute in the iframe. You have successfully triggered XSS. Press Next to finish.

xss-dom.name: XSS: Image Error Vector
xss-dom.description: Trigger XSS using an image tag with an onerror event handler to bypass basic script filters.

steps.text: Many sites filter out <script> tags. Let's use an alternate vector: an image tag. Click the payload input field.
Type this payload: <img src=x onerror=alert('XSS')>
Click Inject. The browser will try to load the invalid image source 'x', fail, and then execute our malicious onerror JavaScript handler instead!
The payload executed! This demonstrates why filtering just script tags is never enough — all user input must be HTML encoded. Press Next to finish.

nmap-basic.name: Basic Scan & Ping Sweep
nmap-basic.description: Learn how to use ping sweeps and basic scans to discover hosts.

steps.text: Welcome to the Nmap Simulator! Let's start by checking if our local machine is responding to pings. Type: ping 127.0.0.1
Great! Now press Enter to execute the ping command.
The host is up. Now let's run a basic Nmap scan on it to see what ports are open. Type: nmap 127.0.0.1
Press Enter to scan.

nmap-sv.name: Service Version Detection
nmap-sv.description: Learn how to use the -sV flag to detect service versions.

steps.text: A basic scan shows open ports, but we need to know exactly what software is running. Type: nmap -sV 127.0.0.1
Press Enter to execute the version scan.

nmap-aggressive.name: Aggressive Scan (-A)
nmap-aggressive.description: Combine OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute.

steps.text: The -A flag is the 'Aggressive' scan. It runs multiple advanced scans at once. Type: nmap -A 127.0.0.1
Press Enter to execute the aggressive scan.

hydra-ssh.name: SSH Brute Force Attack
hydra-ssh.description: Learn how to use Hydra to brute force an SSH login with a password list.

steps.text: Welcome to the Hydra Simulator! Let's start with an SSH brute force attack. First, type 'hydra' to see the usage help.
Press Enter to see Hydra's help output.
Now let's attack an SSH server. We need: -l for the username, -P for the password file, and the target as ssh://IP. Type: hydra -l root -P rockyou.txt ssh://192.168.1.1
Press Enter to launch the brute force attack!
Hydra found the password! In a real scenario, the green line shows the cracked credentials. The -V flag shows every attempt. Try: hydra -l root -P rockyou.txt ssh://192.168.1.1 -V
Press Enter to see verbose mode — each password attempt is logged.

hydra-http.name: HTTP Form Brute Force
hydra-http.description: Learn how to brute force a web application login form using Hydra's http-post-form module.

steps.text: Web application login forms are common brute force targets. Hydra uses the http-post-form module for this. Type the command: hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt shop.local http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"
Press Enter to attack the practice shop login endpoint!

hydra-ftp.name: FTP Brute Force Attack
hydra-ftp.description: Learn how to brute force an FTP server login using Hydra.

steps.text: FTP servers are another common brute force target, especially on legacy systems. The syntax is simple — just change the protocol to ftp://. Type: hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ftp://192.168.1.1
Press Enter to launch the FTP brute force attack!

sqlmap-basic.name: SQLmap: Detect & Enumerate Databases
sqlmap-basic.description: Use the SQLmap simulator to detect SQL injection and list all databases on the target.

steps.text: Welcome to the SQLmap Simulator! First, let's see the help output to understand the tool. Type: sqlmap --help
Press Enter to see SQLmap's full usage guide.
Now let's point SQLmap at a vulnerable URL. The -u flag sets the target URL. Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1"
Press Enter to run the scan. SQLmap will test the 'id' parameter for injection vulnerabilities.
SQLmap confirmed the vulnerability! Now let's list all databases with --dbs. Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1" --dbs
Press Enter to enumerate the databases!

sqlmap-tables.name: SQLmap: Extract Tables from a Database
sqlmap-tables.description: Once you know the database name, use SQLmap to enumerate all tables inside it.

steps.text: We found the database is called 'shopdb'. Now we enumerate its tables with -D and --tables. Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1" -D shopdb --tables
Press Enter. SQLmap will extract the table names from the shopdb database.
We found a 'users' table! Now let's dump it with -T and --dump. Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1" -D shopdb -T users --dump
Press Enter to dump the users table!

sqlmap-fingerprint.name: SQLmap: Database Fingerprinting
sqlmap-fingerprint.description: Gather intelligence about the target DBMS — version, current user, and current database.

steps.text: Before dumping data, it's good practice to fingerprint the DBMS. Let's get the banner (DB version). Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1" --banner
Press Enter to retrieve the database banner.
Now get the current database user (to check privileges). Type: sqlmap -u "http://shop.local/item?id=1" --current-user --current-db
Press Enter to get the current DB user and database name!

net-ftp.name: CTF: Hunt Cleartext Passwords
net-ftp.description: Learn how to filter a massive packet capture to find plaintext FTP credentials.

steps.text: Welcome to the Network Traffic CTF! First, start the live packet stream.
Notice the massive amount of background noise. Let's isolate FTP traffic. Type 'ftp' into the filter bar.
Click Apply to filter the stream.
We found an FTP packet! Click it to inspect its payload and capture the flag.

net-sqli.name: CTF: Detect SQL Injection
net-sqli.description: Learn how to spot a SQL injection attack attempting to steal database records over HTTP.

steps.text: Start the live packet stream.
We suspect a web attack. Filter the traffic for HTTP by typing 'http'.
Click Apply to filter the stream.
You will see several normal HTTP packets and one malicious one containing a UNION SELECT payload. Click the malicious packet to neutralize the threat!

net-beacon.name: CTF: Isolate C2 Beacons
net-beacon.description: Learn how to use TCP port filters to isolate Command and Control (C2) malware beacons.

steps.text: Start the live packet stream.
Malware often communicates over known ports like 4444. Let's filter for this port. Type exactly: tcp.dstport==4444
Click Apply.
Perfect isolation! Click the C2 beacon packet to flag the compromised host.

net-dns.name: CTF: Spot DNS Exfiltration
net-dns.description: Detect data being smuggled out of the network via massive encoded DNS requests.

steps.text: Start the live packet stream.
DNS exfiltration creates huge subdomains. First, filter for DNS traffic by typing 'dns'.
Click Apply.
Look through the filtered DNS list for the packet with a massively long, random-looking subdomain (evil-c2.net). Click it to capture the final flag!
